title: Looking for movies filmed in multiple languages like "Inglourious Basterds", "Everything Everywhere all at Once" or "Call Me By Your Name"

Wes Anderson often uses languages other than English in his movies.

I’ve noticed sometimes his characters seem to understand each other perfectly while speaking two different languages. Zissou and the old man with the posters at the start of Life Aquatic, for example.

The Life Aquatic also features Seu Jorge playing acoustic covers of David Bowie songs in Portuguese.

Singapore Sling is a Greek film, in Greek, French and English. I don't know the details of the production but it being a neo-noir of sorts may have played into the use of different languages, as the director's previous films were all in Greek, from memory. Excellent film, though worth reading about before watching as the content may not be to all tastes.
[removed]

A Body in the woods (Un cos al bosc; 1996) a Catalan film with Rossy de Palma (you may know her from many Pedro almodovar's film) as a Spanish Civil Guard investigating a murder in the Catalan countryside. She plays a police officer; for context, the different Spanish policial corps stopped (most of) their activities and were replaced by Mossos d'Esquadra, the Catalan police. It plays an important part as it does the difference between Catalan and Spanish language. 

[https://letterboxd.com/film/a-body-in-the-woods/](https://letterboxd.com/film/a-body-in-the-woods/)

It's clearly inspired by Twin Peaks and a real criminal case: [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A0sser\_Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alc%C3%A0sser_Girls)

Catalonia: four men on a boar hunt discover the remains of a girl, Montse. The corpse is cut up and daubed 'whore' in blood. The Civil Guard send in an outside investigator, Lt Cifuentes (Rossy de Palma).

The newer asian directors really make good use of it. Minari. The Farewell. Past Lives. Drive My Car (this has the most, including sign!). also Coda? 
French: Anatomy of a Fall. Passages. 
maybe Petzold films? or anything Huppert/Cotillard is in. 
German/Polish/French: Shoah. really interesting seing the languages blend and inform each other. 
Lost in Translation? 
Italian: maybe Rosellini's Journey to Italy where Bergman can't speak the language?

The American Friend (Der amerikanische Freud, 1977) has characters speaking English, German, and French.

Contempt (Le Mépris, 1963) is in French, English, German, and Italian.

Three Colors: White (Trois couleurs: Blanc, 1994) is in French and Polish.
Victoria is in German and English. If you don’t speak German then watch it without subtitles the first time so that it’s more immersive and you can be in the position of the titular character.

Filip (2023): German, French, Yiddish, Polish. It is about hotel employees from all around Europe forced to work in Frankfurt during second war. Main character is Polish Jewish who pretend to be French. It is based on the book of author who this way survived Holocaust.

I’ve always found Wong Kar Wai’s occasional uses of English fascinating.  Days of Being Wild uses multiple languages as well.  Characters in his films sometimes use English to bridge a language barrier, or there’s just characters who outright speak English full time.  But it’s the small moments I find fascinating, where even singular words are said in English.

Bardo, fasle chronicle of a handful of truth could be a great watch for you. It's about a mexican journalist/director who emigrated in USA. Inaritu put a lot of himself in that film. How he managed to live with those two cultures (and languages) is an important theme so you might be interested
Not exactly what you’re looking for but I love how in Bertolucci’s 1900 all the actors cast speak in different languages and are dubbed over for whatever language the film is being released in.

Adding to the Asian ones: Park Chan-Wooks latest falls into this category, with the Handmaiden taking place in japanese-occupied Korea, and Decision to Leave, where the female protagonist is a Chinese immigrant, which the movie makes a number out of.
His movies also regularly switch between Cantonese and Putonghua (Mandarin) - the dialects of Hong Kong and Mainland China - which is something most English viewers don't even notice.
[removed]
Yeah, I never noticed that, but that makes his movies even more interesting.

Ghost Dog has some hilarious scenes with characters apeaking different languages to each other and still kinda having an understanding. Speaking of Jarmusch, Night on Earth is multiple languages but an anthology so maybe that is cheating.

I am huge fan of Abbas Kiarostami's *Certified Copy* from 2011.  He is an Iranian, but the film takes place in Italy.  The main characters are from England and France but they speak English, French, and Italian to each other and other characters in the film.

I think that you would enjoy the film's story as well because the disorienting languages support the disorienting story.

Cheyenne Autumn is a fascinating case of this.

It's a 60s John Ford western centered on the Cheyenne exodus starring real life native Americans. It was meant to be a solemn epic attacking the exploitation and misrepresentation of the natives, mixing English with unsubtitled Cheyenne language.

The thing is that they hired Navajo people to portray the Cheyenne, and who spoke Navajo instead of Cheyenne. The native actors decided to have some fun and filled the film with very crude jokes and nonsensical dialogue that had nothing to do with the plot, with the white filmmakers being none the wiser, and making them legends in the Navajo community.

New Movie Anatomy of a Fall is a great trial film that uses french and english in equal parts

Wages of Fear is an older film that has some english speaking characters but is mostly french

*Anatomy of a Fall* ends up using it as a device for how the intricacies of language can have a major effect on perception. The significance of minor details is amplified when somebody's life is truly on the line.

I really love Devils on the Doorstep. It takes place during the Japanese occupation of China, and translation (and often the lack/misuse of it) plays an integral part to the plot. It's very dark but funny, and of course Jiang Wen is just a phenomenal film maker.

I would also recommend Late Autumn (2010), and Last Life in the Universe. These are quieter/more small scale relationship dramas but so so good.

Joyeux Noël (Merry Christmas) is a French/German/UK co-production. It’s the story of the 1917 Christmas Truce in the trenches of WW1, and is pretty evenly split into French, German, and English (with a Scots dialect.) 

Babylon Berlin is a recent Netflix show that’s predominantly German, but has a fair bit of Russian in it as well. It’s a neo-noir crime drama set in Berlin during the Weimar Republic.

as someone who only speaks mandarin. in his films its about 80% canto and 20% mandarin id say. in the mood for love, some of it was mandarin. fallen angels, all of the voiceover from the mute (Kaneshiro) is in Mandarin, whilst the spoken chinese was all Canto if im remembering correctly. Plus then the Japanese Sushi shop owner spoke Japanese whilst on tape to his son.
fallen angels is mostly Canto but has some Mandarin, Japanese, English dialogue.
That’s crazy.  Does the switch between Canto and Mandarin make it hard for native audiences to understand?

*Godland* does it really well. It switches often between Danish and Icelandic. Given that the movie's premise is about the colonization of Iceland, the language difference plays a prominent role in creating tension and the overarching themes of colonization and "taming" the "noble savages" of Iceland.
[removed]

There was a period where this was popping up in hyperlink cinema. Babel is the most obvious example, with the title even referencing the fact. While English is maybe the most prominent in Babel, just slightly, it’s not even the directors native language. And it has Japanese sign language on top of Japanese in those sequences. 

Syriana has different plots in different languages as well. Traffic, same writer as Syriana, comes to mind. 

Slumdog Millionaire had whole negotiations during production about percentage of each language. Boyle lied to the studio and told them it would be ten percent Hindi when it was slightly over a third. He also brought on Loveleen Tandan as co-director after she translated that third of the script for him to make sure the languages felt real.
[removed]
Drive My Car is a perfect example!

There's a Spanish language version of Dracula, shot on the same sets as the Bela Lugosi version less than 2 weeks later. The director watched the dailies from the Browning film, kept some things and changed others. Not quite the same thing, but you might find it interesting.

Head-On (Gegen die Wand) is in German, Turkish and a little bit of English. The two main characters speak German to each other, speak Turkish to their families (and a friend), and then when the male lead goes to Turkey he actually speaks English with the female lead's cousin (since his Turkish is not that great having grown up in Germany).
And Edge of Heaven, another movie by Fatih Akin, also features dialogue in Turkish, German and English throughout the film.

Quite a few of Kiarostami's films (and also Jafar Panahi's) depict ethnic minorities in Iran, and I think in some of them the minority people seem to be speaking languages other than Farsi. But I don't know any of the languages of the region, so I'm not too sure.

Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence is mostly English but has a lot of Japanese. Apparently the director, Nagisa Oshima, paid a lot of attention to the Japanese actors but let the English actors do whatever they thought was right, which turned out rather well. Great film for the holidays!
